Build an Arithmetic Circuit

VP ≠ VNPAlgebraAlgorithms
Game: Make the target formula out of the inputs using as few steps as possible. Each step adds, subtracts or multiplies two things you already have.
How to play: Choose two wires and an operation, then press Add gate. Reach the target in par to win.

    Look for the math

    An arithmetic circuit is a recipe for computing a polynomial. It starts from the variables and constants, and each gate adds or multiplies two results it already has. Its size is the number of gates. This is the model of computation behind VP and VNP.

    Reuse is the trick

    Written out, x⁸ is eight x's multiplied together, which takes 7 multiplications. A circuit can reuse a result instead: x·x = x², then x²·x² = x⁴, then x⁴·x⁴ = x⁸. That is 3 gates. In the same way (x + 1)³ has four terms but needs only 3 gates. The par for every puzzle here is the true minimum: the logic test tried every circuit with one gate fewer and none of them works. The page Horner's Method shows the same idea for any polynomial in one variable.

    VP and VNP

    Think of a family of polynomials, one for each size n, such as the determinants or the permanents of n × n squares. The family is in VP if circuits whose size grows only like a power of n compute it. The determinant is in VP. The family is in VNP if each coefficient is easy to work out, even when there are exponentially many terms. The permanent is in VNP, and Leslie Valiant proved in 1979 that it is complete for it: if the permanent had small circuits, so would every family in VNP. The question VP ≠ VNP asks whether the permanent really needs huge circuits.

    Two by two is too small to tell

    The 2 × 2 determinant ad − bc and permanent ad + bc both take 3 gates. The difference only shows as the squares grow. The best known circuits for the determinant have about n³ gates (see Determinant by Elimination). The best known for the permanent have about 2ⁿ (see Ryser's Formula).

    Try xy + yz + zx in 4 gates. Hint: two of the three products share a letter.
